transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thanks for seeing me. Um, well, what finally scared me into coming in is that I keep making these really dumb technical mistakes at work. I'm a video editor and camera operator, so details matter, and I just... I know better than to make these errors. Like, I'll label camera cards wrong, or I'll completely miss a timecode note from a director. Recently, I even exported a client cut with the wrong lower-third graphic, and the crazy part is I thought I had checked it. It's just getting to the point where it's affecting my job, and I need to figure out what's going on.
Have you always had trouble with attention and focus, even back in school or earlier jobs, or is this something that's relatively new for you?

It's definitely not new. Um, even way back in elementary school, my teachers actually had to move my desk around a lot. I was just always out of my seat, or I'd blurt out answers, or... I'd be bothering my classmates before I even really realized I was doing it. So, yeah, it's been a problem for basically my whole life.

From elementary school up until now as an adult, would you say these attention and focus problems have been pretty much constant, or have there been times when they got better or went away for a while?

Well, the underlying stuff has always been there, but it hasn't always been this bad. It really got to this level—where it's actually disrupting my work and causing these major mistakes—about two years and two months ago. My company went through a big readjustment, and it completely changed how my shoots are scheduled and how the edit reviews are run. Since then, it's just been a constant struggle to keep it together.
When your company made those big changes two years ago, did your attention and focus problems get worse right around that time, or had they already been getting gradually worse before that happened?

I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. Um... it's kind of hard to say. I just know that right around the time the company changed our schedules and everything, that's when it became really obvious and started actually impacting my work. If it was gradually getting worse before that, I didn't really notice it.

Around the time these work changes happened two years ago, did you start experiencing any feelings of worry, anxiety, or nervousness—either about work specifically or more generally about things in your life?

No, not really. I mean, I was definitely frustrated by the new schedules, but I wouldn't say I was anxious or worried. It wasn't a nervous feeling. It was really just... I was having a much harder time keeping up and staying on track with the edits. But I haven't had any general issues with anxiety or anything like that.

You mentioned being out of your seat and blurting things out in elementary school. Do you still find yourself fidgeting, feeling restless, or having trouble sitting still in situations where you're supposed to—like during meetings or while editing at your desk?

Yeah, I definitely still do. Um, especially in edit reviews. I'm constantly clicking a pen, or bouncing my knee under the table, or just rolling my chair back and forth. It's actually gotten to the point where people have started joking that they can hear me before they even see me.
Going back to when you were in elementary school, were you also fidgeting, bouncing your leg, and feeling restless the way you do now—or is that something that started more recently?

Yeah, it was definitely happening back then too. Um, even in elementary school, my teachers actually had to move my desk because I was always getting out of my seat. I'd be blurting out answers or just bothering my classmates before I even realized I was doing it. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing.
Besides work, do you notice these attention problems and restlessness affecting other areas of your life—like your relationships, managing your home, driving, or social situations?

Um, not really, no. I haven't really noticed it being a problem outside of my job. Like, my relationships and managing the house seem fine. And driving is fine too. I mean, I guess I might still be a little fidgety at home sometimes, but it doesn't cause any real issues with my friends or anything like that. It really just seems to be a problem when I'm trying to get through my editing or sitting in those long meetings.

When you're doing something at home that requires the same kind of sustained attention and detail work as your editing—like maybe following a complex recipe, assembling something, or doing detailed personal projects—do you find yourself making careless mistakes or having trouble focusing the way you do at work?

Um, no, I haven't really noticed that. If I'm doing something around the house, like cooking or putting something together, I don't really make careless mistakes. It's... I don't know, I just don't have that same trouble focusing when it's my own stuff at home. It really just seems to be an issue when I'm at work.

When you're at home watching a movie or reading something that requires you to follow a complex plot or detailed information, do you find yourself getting distracted or having trouble keeping your attention on it the way you might at work?

No, not really. If I'm watching a movie or reading a book at home, I can usually follow along just fine. I don't get distracted or lose track of the plot like I do with the editing stuff at work. It's... yeah, I just don't really have that problem on my own time.

You mentioned that you can follow movies and books fine at home. But what about tasks that are more similar to your editing work—things that require you to sustain focus on technical or detailed information for extended periods, like learning something new from a manual, or doing detailed hobby work that requires precision? Do you find yourself able to maintain that kind of focus?

Um, honestly, I don't really do a lot of that kind of stuff in my free time. But if I do need to, like, read a manual for some new camera gear or figure out something technical for myself, I can get through it fine. I don't find myself zoning out or struggling to focus on it. It really just seems to be the editing and the meetings at work that give me trouble.

When you're working on personal projects that require sustained technical focus—like editing videos for yourself, learning new software, or doing detailed photography work—do you find yourself making careless mistakes or losing focus the way you do at your job?

Um, no, not really. When I'm doing my own photography or, you know, editing my own videos just for fun, I don't lose focus like that. I don't really make careless mistakes on those projects. It really just seems to be a problem when I'm doing it for my actual job.

When you're actually doing the editing work itself—sitting at your desk, reviewing footage, making cuts—do you have the same trouble focusing and making those careless mistakes, or does the problem mainly happen during the meetings and reviews with your team?

Um, it's both, honestly. When I'm sitting at my desk doing the actual editing—like going through the footage and making cuts—that's definitely when I lose focus and make those careless mistakes. But I also struggle during the meetings and reviews. So, yeah, it's not just the meetings, it's the actual editing work too.

Are there any situations outside of work where you're being evaluated or judged by others—like playing sports, performing in front of people, or doing something competitive—where you notice the same kind of trouble focusing and making careless mistakes?

Um, no, not that I can think of. I don't really do a lot of competitive stuff or perform or anything like that. But even if I'm, say, taking photos for a friend's event where they're going to see the results, I don't really have that issue. I stay focused just fine. It really does just seem to be tied to my job.

When you're at work but NOT in meetings or doing editing—like during breaks, casual conversations with coworkers, or less demanding tasks—do you still find yourself fidgeting, restless, and having trouble focusing, or does that mainly happen during the high-pressure editing and review situations?

Um, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really noticed how I am during breaks or just, you know, chatting with coworkers. I guess I've never really thought about whether I'm fidgeting or restless when I'm not actually in the middle of a specific task or a meeting. So, yeah, I can't really say for sure.

During your typical workday, when you're doing routine tasks that don't involve meetings or client reviews—like organizing files, setting up equipment, or doing basic administrative work—do you notice yourself fidgeting, feeling restless, or having trouble staying focused on those tasks?

Um, I don't really know. I guess I haven't paid much attention to how I act when I'm just organizing files or doing paperwork. I mean, maybe I do fidget a little, but I really couldn't say for sure if it's any worse than usual. I just haven't noticed.

Let me ask this more directly: When you're NOT at work—like at home, with friends, or doing personal activities—do you generally feel restless, fidgety, or like you have trouble sitting still, or does that mainly happen at work?

Honestly, I'm just not sure about at home, either. When I'm off the clock—like hanging out with friends or just relaxing in my living room—I'm not really paying attention to my body language or whether I'm sitting perfectly still. I'm just... living my life, I guess. I haven't really thought to look out for whether I'm feeling restless when I'm in my own space. So I really can't give you a clear yes or no on that.

When you're sitting on your couch at home in the evening, just relaxing by yourself with no work pressure, do you find yourself fidgeting with your hands, bouncing your leg, or feeling like you need to move around—or are you able to sit comfortably and still?

I don't really know. Like I said, I just don't pay attention to that kind of thing when I'm at home. If I'm on the couch watching TV or whatever, I'm just watching TV. I don't know if my leg is bouncing or if I'm messing with my hands. I've just never really stopped to think about it or look for it.

I want to circle back to something. You mentioned your teachers had to move your desk in elementary school because you were out of your seat. When you were a kid, outside of school—like at home, at the dinner table, or during family activities—were you also getting up and moving around a lot, or was that mainly a school problem?

To be honest, I remember the school stuff a lot more clearly than how I was at home. Like you said, the teachers did move my desk, but it wasn't just because I was out of my seat. It was also because I was always blurting out answers, or... well, bothering my classmates before I even realized I was doing it. 

So school was definitely a big issue. I don't really remember if I was getting up a lot at the dinner table or during family stuff, but I definitely remember getting in trouble for doing all of that in class.
